name: App Review 5.1.1 and 5.1.2 data rules
plain: Apple's review rules: collect only needed data, say why, ask consent, and do not track without ATT.
meaning: 5.1.1 covers privacy policy, consent, data minimization, permission purpose strings and account deletion. 5.1.2 covers data use and sharing, ATT and the ban on building profiles or fingerprinting. Reviews are the real enforcement.

android.note: Play User Data policy is the equivalent; see Data safety and permissions entries.

ios.store_policy: 5.1.1(i) policy link, (ii) consent, (iii) minimization, (v) account deletion; 5.1.2(i) no sharing without permission, ATT, no fingerprinting
ios.api_surface: App Store review, purpose strings in Info.plist
ios.note: Guideline text changes several times a year; always check the live page.

limits.headline: Can't collect data or track you in ways that break App Store review
limits.user_action: Nothing for you to do. The rules are checked when the developer submits the app
can: Collect data it needs, with a privacy policy and your consent
Explain why in the permission text
Ask to track across apps through the Allow or Ask App Not to Track box
cannot: Build a profile of you or fingerprint your phone
Track you after you said no, without being rejected
Skip account deletion if it has accounts
limits.differs: These are Apple rules for iPhone. Google Play has its own User Data policy for Android.

story.what_it_is: Apple's rules on what data an app may collect, how to ask, and how not to track.

marketing.name: App Review Guidelines, Privacy
marketing.pitch: Apps must collect only what they need, say why, ask permission and respect tracking choices.

story.for_you: You see clear permission asks, a privacy policy link and a delete button. If an app tries to track you after you said no, it can be removed from the store.
story.for_makers: Reviewers check consent, purpose strings, account deletion and data sharing. Makers must plan data collection around the rules or be rejected, so design and legal teams read these lines closely.

use_cases.example: A new social app is rejected until it adds a privacy policy link and a clear reason for each prompt.
A game cannot require a login or personal details just to play a single player level.
An ad network that ignores a No on tracking risks having its apps pulled.
A kids app drops behavioral ads and some analytics to qualify for the Kids category.
A health app must clearly say it will not sell your health data to advertisers.
A shopping app is rejected for forcing sign up before showing prices.

story.android_note: Google's Play policies cover similar ground but with different forms.
story.ios_note: iOS rules also ban rebuilding a hidden ID from device signals to track people who said no.

history.change: Account deletion and ATT rules added in guidelines
Privacy manifest and required reason rules referenced
